pages.title: Headless claude -p persists sessions: three-layer fix for compounding re-ingestion
pages.summary: Every headless claude -p run was writing its own transcript under ~/.claude/projects, which the nightly collector then re-ingested the next night, compounding cost. Fixed with three independent layers so the bug can't come back silently.
pages.body_html:
Root cause

A nightly extraction loop got more expensive every day with no matching increase in real work. Cause: claude -p persists a session transcript even in headless/scripted use, under ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/. The loop ran from a fresh $TMPDIR/loopwatch.XXXXXX each night, so each run created a new project dir (e.g. -private-var-folders-...-T-loopwatch-a1B2c3) containing the entire input bundle it was fed — a one-word test reply alone produced a 231 KB transcript. The collector's glob (~/.claude/projects/*/*.jsonl) then picked that transcript up on night N+1, so each run re-mined the prior night's input. Cost compounds silently because nothing errors — it just keeps growing.

Fix: three independent layers

  1. Suppress persistence at the source. Pass --no-session-persistence (verified on claude 2.1.283: no project dir is created at all).
  2. Run from a fixed directory and exclude it. Always invoke from ~/.local/state/loopwatch/run (not a fresh tmpdir), and exclude its encoded project-dir name from collection — every non-alphanumeric character in the path becomes - — plus anything ending in -loopwatch-run, and the old v0.1 loopwatch-XXXXXX mktemp dirs for backward compatibility.
  3. Filter by cwd field at ingestion time. Drop any transcript line whose cwd field equals the run dir. This is the safety net that catches a moved or renamed project dir even if layers 1–2 fail.

Tradeoff of layer 2: a fixed run dir means runs must be serialized (no two loopwatch runs concurrently). An existing mkdir-based lock already enforced this, so it was free.

Related: budget enforcement is fail-closed

--max-budget-usd is real and enforced: a run capped at 0.05 that actually cost 0.066 returned is_error:true with exit 1 rather than silently overspending. Decision: treat a budget hit as a failed run — hold watermarks and record a ledger row with skipped_reason=budget_exceeded — rather than advancing state, otherwise the same delta would just burn budget again next run without ever completing.

Gotchas

  • On macOS, /var is a symlink to /private/var, so the path-encoded project-dir name you compute may not match what the CLI actually creates. The suffix-match rule (layer 2) exists specifically to survive this.
  • Verify persistence behavior against the actual CLI version in use — flag behavior was confirmed empirically on 2.1.283, not assumed from docs.

pages.title: Redaction for unattended pipelines: pre-model scrub + post-output scan with fail-closed drops
pages.summary: Secrets and client names are scrubbed via a gitignored redact.list before any model sees the data, then the model's own output is re-scanned and any page that still matches gets dropped rather than published.
pages.body_html:
Pattern

For a headless pipeline that feeds real transcripts to an LLM and publishes what comes back, redaction has to happen twice, at two different trust boundaries:

  • Before the model sees anything: a gitignored redact.list (patterns keyed by kind, e.g. redact.list:1) is compiled into regexes and applied to the bundle first. Matches are replaced with [REDACTED:<kind>] markers, never left as-is and never partially reconstructible.
  • After the model writes output: the same scan runs again over the generated pages before publish. This is fail-closed: if a page still matches a secret pattern or a redaction-list term anywhere — body, title, summary, tags, or slug — that specific page file is deleted from the output rather than published. One bad page doesn't block the rest of the run.

The list itself lives outside version control (gitignored) so the patterns that define what's sensitive never end up in a public repo alongside the tool that enforces them.

Why both layers

Pre-model scrubbing keeps raw secrets out of any prompt or model context in the first place — the model literally never sees them. Post-output scanning is the backstop for cases the pre-scrub missed (paraphrasing, partial reconstruction, or a pattern that only becomes recognizable once summarized). Relying on either layer alone leaves a gap: pre-scrub misses novel leaks the model itself introduces; post-scan alone would mean secrets briefly transited the model.

README framing

The privacy posture is stated plainly rather than implied: "Privacy is enforced, not advised" — i.e., this is a hard filter with fail-closed behavior on the publish path, not a prompt instruction the model is trusted to honor unassisted.

Gotchas

  • Fail-closed means a legitimate page can be silently dropped if it happens to match a pattern coincidentally (e.g. a term that looks like a redacted client name but isn't). Worth logging drops distinctly from normal skips so false positives are discoverable.
  • The redaction-list file must stay out of git; if it's ever committed, the list of what's considered sensitive becomes public alongside the scrubber that's supposed to protect it.

pages.title: Byte-offset watermarking: three correctness bugs (partial lines, truncation, path leaks)
pages.summary: Phase 1 fixed three watermark bugs in the log-collection layer: stopping at the last complete newline instead of file size, resetting on file truncation, and hashing dir keys instead of storing absolute paths.
pages.body_html:
Bugs and fixes

  • Partial-line loss. The watermark previously advanced to the file's current size, which can land mid-line if a writer is flushing incrementally. Reading from that offset next time skips the second half of a truncated line and permanently loses it. Fix: advance the watermark only to the last complete newline seen, never past it, so a partially-written line is re-read (and completed) on the next pass instead of being silently dropped.
  • No reset on truncation. If a source file shrinks (log rotation, a fixture being rewritten smaller) and the new size is less than the stored watermark, reading from the old offset would either fail or return garbage/wrong data. Fix: detect size < old_watermark and reset the watermark to 0 for that file, treating it as a fresh file rather than trusting a now-invalid offset.
  • Path leaks in git. Watermark state was originally keyed by the absolute source path, which could embed a client or project name (e.g. from a cwd-derived project directory) directly into a file that gets committed. Fix: key watermark entries by a hash of the path instead of the raw path, so committed state carries no human-readable identifying strings.

Why this matters

Watermarking is the mechanism that makes the whole pipeline incremental and idempotent — get any one of these wrong and you either silently lose data (partial-line loss, no reset on truncation) or leak identifying information into version control (path leaks). All three are the kind of bug that looks fine in a smoke test with clean, static fixtures and only shows up against real, growing, occasionally-rotated log files.

Gotchas

  • Truncation reset assumes shrink always means "new file" — if a source can legitimately shrink and grow back while representing the same logical stream, this will cause re-processing of old data instead of a true reset.
  • Hashing the key means watermark state files are no longer human-readable for debugging; keep a separate (gitignored) mapping if you need to inspect which hash corresponds to which real path.
